opus-5.5.text:
I think Holden's influence was enormous, and it's a little hard to overstate. A lot of what made Open Phil's AI strategy work distinctive came from his personal temperament as a thinker. He has this instinct to not take the conventional framing of a question for granted, and to keep asking, "Okay, but what do we actually believe here, and why?" He was never satisfied with a vibe or a consensus view. He wanted to see the argument laid out, and he wanted to know which parts were load-bearing.

In practice, that meant he pushed the research team toward what I'd call "big picture worldview investigations." Instead of only making grants within a field as it already existed, he wanted us to step back and ask foundational questions. When might transformative AI arrive? How likely is it to be dangerous? What would the world look like if it went well or badly? Those questions are huge and messy, and a lot of people would say they're too speculative to make progress on. Holden's view was roughly that if we're going to allocate a lot of money and attention based on these beliefs, we'd better try hard to make them as rigorous as we can, even if we can't get anywhere near certainty.

My own biological anchors report is a good example. Holden was very involved in shaping what question it was trying to answer, and in pressure-testing it along the way. He had a way of reading a draft and identifying the one assumption you'd been quietly leaning on without defending it. That could be painful, but it made the work much better.

He also modeled a certain intellectual honesty that I think rubbed off on the culture. He'd write publicly about where he'd changed his mind, and he'd be explicit about his uncertainty instead of projecting confidence he didn't have. That made it feel safe for researchers to say, "I don't know," or "I think I was wrong about this." In a field where the questions are this hard, that's essential.

The flip side is that because so much of the depth depended on his personal engagement, there's a fair question about how much of that research culture can persist when someone like him isn't in the room driving it. I think a lot of it did get absorbed into how people at Open Phil think, but it really was his fingerprints all over it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think Holden's influence is hard to overstate, honestly. When I joined Open Phil, the way we thought about AI was still pretty high-level and philosophical in a lot of ways, and Holden was really the person pushing for us to make the case concrete. His attitude was basically: if we're going to make big bets on transformative AI being a real possibility this century, we owe it to ourselves and to the people we're trying to persuade to actually spell out the argument in detail, with numbers, with models, with explicit assumptions you can push back on.

The biological anchors work is a good example. That project came out of Holden saying something like, "I keep telling people I think there's a meaningful chance of transformative AI in the next few decades, and I don't have a crisp account of why. Can you go figure out whether that's actually defensible?" And he wasn't satisfied with a quick memo. He wanted a report where every step was laid out so a skeptic could say, "Okay, I disagree with this specific parameter," rather than just, "that sounds like sci-fi." That was really his push, and it shaped how I approached the whole thing.

The other thing I'd say is that he has this habit of being his own harshest critic. He's really willing to say, "I think our previous view was wrong, here's why, here's what changed." That set a culture where the research wasn't about defending a position, it was about getting closer to the truth and being transparent about uncertainty. His "most important century" series is sort of the public-facing version of that, where he took a lot of the internal research and tried to walk through it honestly, including the parts that felt weird or uncomfortable to say out loud.

So I'd put it as: he raised the bar on rigor, he insisted on legibility, and he modeled intellectual honesty in a way that made the rest of us feel like it was okay to be wrong in public as long as you were being careful. I think a lot of the depth you see in Open Phil's AI work traces back to that.

astra-6.text:
My sense is that Holden has had a huge influence on that. He’s unusually willing to spend a long time unpacking a question that sounds simple, like, “When might AI become transformative?” or “What would actually help?” And he pushes you to make the reasoning explicit: what are you assuming, why do you believe it, and would changing that assumption change the decision?

That gives researchers both permission to go deep and a reason to keep the work connected to decisions. The point isn’t just to produce an interesting analysis; it’s to understand what we should do differently. I wouldn’t attribute all of OpenPhil’s research depth to one person, but I think that combination has been a big part of his influence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Holden had a huge influence on the depth of that work. He was very willing to keep asking, “What would we actually need to believe for this strategy to make sense?” And if the answer depended on some really difficult question about AI, he was willing to have us spend a substantial amount of time trying to understand it.

That matters because there’s a natural pressure in philanthropy to get to the grants—to make decisions and move money. Holden really valued stepping back and examining the assumptions behind those decisions. He also pushed for explanations that he could interrogate himself, rather than just deferring to someone’s bottom line. I think that combination of patience and very persistent questioning helped make the research much deeper.
